passages.happening:
The chapter opens with one long case. A man marries a woman. She ‘becomes displeasing to him because he finds some indecency in her’. He writes her ‘a certificate of divorce’, hands it to her, and sends her away (verse 1).

She marries another man. That marriage also ends, by divorce or by his death (verses 2-3).

Then comes the ruling, which is the only command in the passage. In that case ‘the husband who divorced her first may not remarry her after she has been defiled, for that is an abomination to the LORD’ (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
Read closely, this law does not set up divorce and does not praise it. The first three verses only describe what happens. Divorce is taken as a fact of life in that world. The single command is in verse 4, and it is a limit.

Divorce by a written document was known across the ancient world. The certificate protected the woman. It proved that she was free, so that she could marry again without being accused of adultery. The Hebrew word for it comes from a root meaning to cut off.

The words translated ‘some indecency’ are, word for word, a nakedness of a thing, and their meaning was argued over in ancient times. They point to something shameful. They probably do not mean adultery, which had its own penalty in chapter 22. By the first century two schools of Jewish teachers read the phrase in opposite ways. The school of Shammai held that it meant sexual unfaithfulness. The school of Hillel allowed divorce for much smaller causes. That argument is the background to the question the Pharisees put to Jesus.

Why may the first husband not take her back? Interpreters differ. Some think the rule protected the woman from being treated like goods, sent away and reclaimed at a man's whim. Others think a return after a second marriage was seen as a kind of adultery. The words ‘after she has been defiled’ are hard. They may describe how the first husband had treated her when he sent her away.

Whatever the reason, the effect was to make a man think before he wrote the certificate. He could not send his wife away lightly and expect to have her back.
passages.later:
The prophet Malachi speaks God's mind about a man who discards his wife: “So guard yourselves in your spirit and do not break faith” (Malachi 2:16).

The Pharisees asked Jesus why Moses had ordered a man ‘to give his wife a certificate of divorce and send her away’ (Matthew 19:7). Jesus corrected one word. “Moses permitted you to divorce your wives because of your hardness of heart; but it was not this way from the beginning” (Matthew 19:8). He took them behind Deuteronomy to Genesis: “Therefore what God has joined together, let man not separate” (Matthew 19:6).
passages.hard:
Does this passage approve of divorce? And what do Christians say about divorce and remarriage?

The passage regulates divorce. It does not command it. Jesus reads it in that way. He calls it something Moses ‘permitted’ because of hard hearts, and he says it was not God's purpose from the beginning.

Beyond that, Christians differ, and the note on Matthew 19 sets out the views. The Catholic Church teaches that a true sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved while both spouses live. The Orthodox churches hold marriage to be for life but, as an act of mercy, allow a second marriage. Most Protestant churches hold that unfaithfulness and desertion can free the innocent partner to remarry, and many also count abuse as breaking the marriage covenant. These notes do not decide between them.

What all of them share is Jesus' main point. God meant marriage to last for life, and divorce is always a tearing of what he joined. In his world, Jesus' words also protected wives, who could be sent away with almost no say.

Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger. If you are in an abusive marriage, seek safety first. Talk to a pastor or a counselor you trust, or call a local domestic violence line. These notes are not legal advice. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The law made a man stop and think before he sent his wife away. Ask whether there is a promise you are treating as easy to undo. And if you carry the pain of a marriage that has ended, hear that this passage was written to limit harm, and that Jesus' words were spoken to protect the one who was being discarded.

passages.t: A year at home, a millstone, and a stolen person
passages.happening:
Short laws follow, each guarding something a person cannot live without.

A newly married man is not to be sent to war or burdened with public duty. “For one year he is free to stay at home and bring joy to the wife he has married” (verse 5).

No one may take a pair of millstones, or even the upper stone, as security for a loan, ‘because that would be taking one’s livelihood as security’ (verse 6).

A man who kidnaps a fellow Israelite, ‘whether he treats him as a slave or sells him’, must die (verse 7).

And in cases of skin disease, Israel is to do what the priests instruct. “Remember what the LORD your God did to Miriam” (verses 8-9).
passages.hearers:
The first law is one of the most tender in the book. A new marriage is given a year of peace. The state may not claim the husband. And the purpose is stated from the wife's side. He is to ‘bring joy’ to her.

The millstones. Every household had a small hand mill of two stones. Each day's grain was ground on it for each day's bread. To take it as a pledge was to take the family's next meal. A lender may ask for security. He may not ask for the thing that keeps the borrower alive.

Kidnapping. To seize a person and make him a slave, or sell him, is punished by death. The law treats the theft of a human being as an attack on life. This is the practice on which the slave trade of later centuries was built, and the law of Moses forbids it outright.

Miriam. Numbers 12 tells how the sister of Moses spoke against him and was struck with a skin disease for seven days. Moses reminds Israel of it as a reason to take the priests' directions seriously. The Leviticus notes say plainly that such diseases were not sin and were not a cause for shame. Miriam's is one particular story. It is not a rule for reading anyone's illness.
passages.later:
Exodus gives the law against kidnapping in its first form: “Whoever kidnaps another man must be put to death, whether he sells him or the man is found in his possession” (Exodus 21:16).

Paul lists ‘slave traders’ among those who act against sound teaching (1 Timothy 1:10).

The book of Job describes the wicked as people who ignore the spirit of verse 6: they ‘take the widow’s ox in pledge’ (Job 24:3).
passages.asks: The law would not let a lender take the thing a family needed to eat. Ask whether any claim you press on another person takes what they cannot live without. And notice the year given to a new marriage. Ask what your closest relationships have been given, in time and attention, to make them strong.

passages.t: The poor man's cloak and the worker's wages
passages.happening:
Two laws protect the poor in their dealings with those who have more.

The first is about loans. “When you lend anything to your neighbor, do not enter his house to collect security. You are to stand outside while the man to whom you are lending brings the security out to you” (verses 10-11). If he is poor and the pledge is his cloak, it must go back to him by sunset, ‘so that he may sleep in his own cloak and bless you’ (verse 13).

The second is about pay. “Do not oppress a hired hand who is poor and needy, whether he is a brother or a foreigner residing in one of your towns. You are to pay his wages each day before sunset, because he is poor and depends on them. Otherwise he may cry out to the LORD against you, and you will be guilty of sin” (verses 14-15).
passages.hearers:
Both laws turn on sunset. By evening the cloak must be back, and by evening the wage must be paid.

The lender at the door. A man who owes money has already lost much of his standing. This law keeps the rest. The lender may not walk into the borrower's house and pick out what he wants. He waits outside. The poor man's home is still his own, and he chooses what to bring out.

The cloak. A poor man's outer garment was also his blanket. If it was all he had to offer as security, the lender could hold it by day and had to return it at night. A pledge that goes home every evening is hardly a pledge at all. That is the point. The law makes lending to the very poor close to an act of trust.

The wage. A day laborer had no land and no store of food. He lived on what he earned that day, and his family ate that night on what he brought home. To hold his pay until morning was to send them to bed hungry. The law names the worker's position twice: he is ‘poor and needy’, and he ‘depends on’ his pay.

The law protects the foreign worker in the same words as the Israelite. And it says where the worker's complaint goes if no court will hear it. He ‘may cry out to the LORD against you’. God counts unpaid wages as sin.

Verse 13 says that returning the cloak ‘will be credited to you as righteousness’. Righteousness, in this book, looks like a poor man asleep under his own blanket.
passages.later:
Leviticus gives the same law of wages: “You must not withhold until morning the wages due a hired hand” (Leviticus 19:13).

James speaks to rich landowners in the words of verse 15: “Look, the wages you withheld from the workmen who mowed your fields are crying out against you. The cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of Hosts” (James 5:4).

Jesus told a story about a landowner who paid his workers at evening, as this law requires, and who gave the last ones hired a full day's pay (Matthew 20:8-9).
passages.asks: The law thinks about what a delay costs the person waiting. Ask who is waiting for something you owe: pay, a decision, or an answer. And ask whether your dealings with people who are in your debt leave them their dignity.

passages.t: Each for his own sin, and what is left in the field
passages.happening:
A principle of justice is stated. “Fathers shall not be put to death for their children, nor children for their fathers; each is to die for his own sin” (verse 16).

Justice is not to be denied to the foreigner or the fatherless, and a widow's cloak is not to be taken as a pledge. “Remember that you were slaves in Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you from that place” (verses 17-18).

Then the harvest. A sheaf forgotten in the field is not to be fetched. Olive trees are not to be beaten a second time, and vines are not to be picked over again. Each time the law says the same thing: ‘What remains will be for the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow’ (verses 19-21).

“Remember that you were slaves in the land of Egypt. Therefore I am commanding you to do this” (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
Verse 16 limits punishment to the one who did the wrong. In the ancient world a man's family could be made to suffer with him. Israel's courts are forbidden to do that. A child is not guilty of a parent's crime.

This verse is important for reading the hardest pages of the Bible. It is God's own rule for human justice, and it is the reason a reader is troubled when children die in the wars of these books. The Bible itself taught that conscience.

The foreigner, the fatherless and the widow are named together four times in these few verses. They were the people most likely to fall through the gaps of a society built on family land. They had no land, no harvest, and often no one to speak for them in court.

The gleaning laws give them a share in every harvest. Harvest was done by hand. The farmer is told not to be thorough. What he misses, he leaves. The poor may then come into the field and gather it.

This is not charity handed down. The poor gather it with their own hands, and they take what the law says is theirs. It leaves them their dignity. And it asks something of the owner's heart. He must let go of the idea that every last olive on his own tree belongs to him.

The reason is given twice, at verse 18 and verse 22, like a frame around the whole section. Israel had been slaves. A people that remembers what it was to have nothing will leave something in the field.
passages.later:
King Amaziah obeyed verse 16. When he punished the men who had murdered his father, ‘he did not put the sons of the murderers to death, but acted according to what is written in the Book of the Law of Moses’ (2 Kings 14:6).

The prophet Ezekiel preached a whole chapter on the principle: “The soul who sins is the one who will die” (Ezekiel 18:4).

The book of Ruth shows the gleaning law at work. Ruth, a widow and a foreigner, asked, “Please let me go into the fields and glean heads of grain” (Ruth 2:2). The owner of the field, Boaz, went beyond the law and told his men, ‘pull out for her some stalks from the bundles and leave them for her to gather’ (Ruth 2:16).
passages.asks: The farmer was told to leave the edges of his success for people with nothing. Ask what the edges of your field are: the part of your income, your time or your skill that you could leave for others to gather. And ask whether the way you help people leaves them their dignity.
